title: Amyraut on evil acts: an external and an internal act of providence
source_text: L. Similiter quoad actus malos, circa eos docet esse duplicem Providentiae actum, unum externum, & alterum internum. Et externum quidem dicit circa duo occupari. Vel enim, inquit, versatur in propositione objectorum, quae facultates commovere idonea sunt: Vel in eo consistit, quod Deus nihil agit quidem, sed sinit & patitur Diabolum ἐνέργειαν suam explicare, ut objectorum efficacitatem adjuvet. Internus autem Dei actus, qui in malis hominum operibus intervenit, in eo juxta ipsum consistit, quod Deus ex pluribus objectis ad malum inducentibus, quae homo in mente agitat, unum vel obscurat, vel omnino ex mente eripit, aut etiam unum aliquod objectum ab ea parte offerri procurat, qua est maxime aptum, & idoneum ad movendum. In quibus omnibus pariter nihil potest officere humanae libertati.
pass_a_gloss: Similarly as to evil acts, he teaches that about them there is a twofold act of Providence, one external, and the other internal. And the external he says is occupied about two things. For either, he says, it is engaged in the proposition of objects, which are fit to stir the faculties: Or it consists in this, that God does nothing indeed, but permits and suffers the Devil to unfold his energeia, that he may help the efficacy of the objects. But the internal act of God, which intervenes in the evil works of men, consists according to him in this, that God of many objects inducing to evil, which man turns over in his mind, either obscures one, or snatches it altogether from the mind, or even procures that some one object be offered from that side, by which it is most apt, and fit for moving. In all which equally nothing can hurt human liberty.
pass_b_english: In the same way, with respect to evil acts, he teaches that Providence acts in two ways, one external and the other internal. The external act, he says, concerns two things. 'Either it is engaged in presenting objects fitted to stir the faculties, or it consists in this: God does nothing himself, but allows and permits the devil to exercise his working, so as to add to the force of the objects.'

God's internal act in the evil deeds of human beings consists, according to him, in this: out of the many objects leading to evil that a person turns over in his mind, God either obscures one or removes it from the mind altogether, or else arranges for some one object to be presented from the side on which it is most apt and suited to move. In none of this, likewise, can there be anything harmful to human freedom.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
